Duration metrics are recorded under the wrong store or label
Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` when the Storage call fails, so the failure is counted against legacy. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine (line 166) calls `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy latency and errors are counted as storage. Delete's success path (line 106) passes `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`, which adds a high-cardinality label value.
Storage failures show up as legacy failures, legacy delete-collection results are mixed into the storage series, and the de

Async legacy writes run on the request context, so they are cancelled when the request ends
Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection now start a goroutine for the legacy write and return right after. The goroutine builds its timeout context from `ctx`, which is the request-scoped context (lines 50-51, 108-110, 134-135 and 161-163). When the handler returns, the API server cancels that context. The legacy call is then usually cancelled or fails with `context canceled`. The 10s timeout never applies, because the parent is cancelled first. The legacy write is no longer guaranteed to happen. Co

Delete stores d.Log in the context instead of the enriched logger
Line 97 calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of passing the `log` built on line 96. The name, kind and method values are therefore missing from the logs of downstream calls that read the logger from the context. Create, Get, List, Update and DeleteCollection all pass `log`.
Logs from Storage.Delete and Legacy.Delete lack the request-specific fields, which makes them harder to trace.

judge_pairs.reason: Both flag recordLegacyDuration being called when the Storage operation fails, where the storage duration should be recorded.
Both flag Delete's metric passing name instead of options.Kind.
Both flag Delete using klog.NewContext with d.Log instead of the enriched log variable.

These look like leftover debugging statements. They run at Error level. Each batch writes up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs, and the loop runs until no rows are left.
Every cleanup run writes large error-level log lines for successful work. This floods logs and error alerting, and it can write very large lines when the batch size

Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
Run now ticks every minute instead of every 10 minutes. Each tick runs clean(), which uses a 9-minute timeout and runs all cleanup jobs. This looks like a debugging leftover and is not tied to the annotation change.
Heavy cleanup jobs (annotations, dashboard versions, and others) run ten times as often. This adds database load and can overlap with a previous run that is still in progress.

judge_pairs.reason: Both flag debug-style logging emitted at Error level in annotation cleanup, polluting production error logs.

comment_verdicts.text:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false and inverts the feature flag
enableSqlExpressions assigns `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, which negates the flag. It then returns false when `enabled` is true, and also returns false on the fall-through. Every path returns false, so the feature flag has no effect. In ReadQuery, the QueryTypeSQL case therefore always returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented", even when the flag is turned on. I found no performance problem on the changed path. The stubbed DB methods in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return immediately and do no work

judge_pairs.reason: Both say enableSqlExpressions always returns false, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions regardless of the feature flag.
